passages.t: ‘I am jealous for you with a godly jealousy’
passages.happening:
Paul asks the church to put up with a little foolishness from him (verse 1). Then he says why he cares so much. “I am jealous for you with a godly jealousy. For I promised you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (verse 2).

He is afraid. “I am afraid, however, that just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning, your minds may be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ” (verse 3).

The danger is real. Someone has come preaching “a Jesus other than the One we proclaimed”, or “a different gospel than the one you accepted”, and they “put up with it way too easily” (verse 4).

Paul says he is “in no way inferior to those” whom he calls, with irony, ‘super-apostles’ (verse 5). He is not a polished speaker, but he is not lacking in knowledge (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Paul pictures himself as the father of a bride. In Jewish custom, a betrothal was a binding promise, much stronger than an engagement today. Joseph and Mary were betrothed, and Matthew calls Joseph “her husband” before the wedding (Matthew 1:19). The father's task was to keep his daughter for her husband and present her on the wedding day. Paul brought the Corinthians to Christ. Now he wants to hand them over whole, not stolen by someone else.

‘Godly jealousy’ is not envy. It is the protective love of someone who will not share the one he loves with a rival.

‘A Jesus other than the One we proclaimed’ is a strong charge. Paul does not say exactly what the newcomers taught. But in these chapters their Jesus seems to be one of success and show, not of the cross and weakness. Who they were is not known for sure. The book page's part ‘The ‘super-apostles’’ sets out the main views.

‘Super-apostles’ is irony. Paul uses their own high claims against them. ‘Not a polished speaker’ uses a word for an ordinary person without trained skill. Paul admits he lacked the speaking style Corinth admired. He does not admit he lacked the truth.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament often pictures God as the husband of his people. Isaiah tells Israel, “For your husband is your Maker” (Isaiah 54:5), and Hosea hears God say, “So I will betroth you to Me forever; I will betroth you in righteousness and justice, in loving devotion and compassion” (Hosea 2:19).

God's jealousy is part of that love. “For you must not worship any other god, for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God” (Exodus 34:14).

Verse 3 points back to the garden. The serpent “was more crafty than any beast of the field” (Genesis 3:1), and Eve said, “The serpent deceived me” (Genesis 3:13). The note on Genesis 3:1-7 tells that story. Paul's point is not about women. It is about how false words can sound reasonable and still pull a heart away from God.
passages.asks: Paul feared the Corinthians would lose their ‘simple and pure devotion to Christ’. Ask what tends to pull your heart away from Christ: not always something evil, but something that crowds him out. And ask how you can tell when a teaching offers a different Jesus from the one in the Gospels.

passages.happening:
Paul asks a sharp question. “Was it a sin for me to humble myself in order to exalt you, because I preached the gospel of God to you free of charge?” (verse 7).

Other churches, in Macedonia, had paid his way while he served Corinth. “I robbed other churches by accepting their support in order to serve you” (verse 8). He will keep refusing to be a burden to them (verse 9). Why? Not because he does not love them. “God knows I do!” (verse 11).

He will keep doing it, to take away any ground for his rivals to claim they are his equals (verse 12).

Then he names them plainly. “For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light” (verses 13 and 14). So it is not surprising if his servants pretend too. “Their end will correspond to their actions” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
In Corinth, to take money from a rich member could make a teacher that person's client, someone who owed him loyalty and belonged to his circle. Many travelling teachers lived off their hearers. Paul worked with his hands (Acts 18:3) and took gifts only from churches he was not living among at the time (Philippians 4:15-16). Some in Corinth seem to have felt insulted. A real apostle, they thought, would accept their support. Paul says his refusal was love.

Paul does not say that paid ministers are wrong. In his first letter he defended the right of apostles to be supported (1 Corinthians 9:14). He chose not to use that right in Corinth.

‘Masquerading’ is metaschēmatizō, to change one's outward form, to wear a disguise. It comes three times in three verses: the false apostles, Satan, and his servants. The outside looks like light and righteousness. The inside does not match.

Where did the picture of Satan as ‘an angel of light’ come from? Paul does not say. A Jewish retelling of the story of Adam and Eve, whose date is not certain, tells of Satan taking the bright form of an angel to deceive Eve. Whether Paul knew that story is not known. It would fit his mention of Eve in verse 3.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament warns about prophets who look right and speak falsely. “The prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests rule by their own authority. My people love it so” (Jeremiah 5:31).

Ezekiel condemns shepherds who use the flock for themselves: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed their flock?” (Ezekiel 34:2).

Jesus gave the same warning: “Beware of false prophets. They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves. By their fruit you will recognize them” (Matthew 7:15-16).

And in Job, the accuser comes among the sons of God as if he belonged there (Job 1:6).
passages.hard:
Who were the ‘false apostles’, and may Christians call others by that name?

Paul does not name them. We know them only from this letter. They were Jewish Christian teachers, as Paul was (verse 22). They carried letters of recommendation, spoke well, took money, and boasted of visions. Most readers think the ‘super-apostles’ of verse 5 and the ‘false apostles’ of verse 13 are the same people. A few think the ‘super-apostles’ were the leaders in Jerusalem whose names the newcomers used. The book page sets out these views and does not choose. Paul's quarrel is with their way of ministry and their ‘different gospel’, not with who they were by birth. He shared it.

‘Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light’ is a warning. Evil does not usually look evil. A teacher can seem gifted, warm, spiritual and successful, and still use a church for his own gain. Paul tells us how to see it: look at what such teachers do to people, as verse 20 shows, and at which Jesus they preach.

But these verses are not a licence to call any Christian we disagree with a false apostle or a servant of Satan. Paul names people who preached another gospel and preyed on a church. Christians who differ over many things are still brothers and sisters. The warning is for real wolves, not for every argument.
passages.asks: Paul refused money so that the gospel would be free and no one could doubt his motives. Ask what it would cost you to serve without getting anything back. Then ask how you judge a teacher: by how impressive they seem, or by the Jesus they preach and how they treat people.

passages.happening:
Paul says again that he is about to act like a fool. “But if you do, then receive me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little” (verse 16). He is not speaking as the Lord would, but as a fool (verse 17). Since many boast in human terms, he will too (verse 18).

Then comes biting irony. “For you gladly tolerate fools, since you are so wise” (verse 19).

He shows them what they have put up with. “In fact, you even put up with anyone who enslaves you or exploits you or takes advantage of you or exalts himself or strikes you in the face” (verse 20).

And he ends with more irony. “To my shame I concede that we were too weak for that!” (verse 21). But if others will boast, he can match them.
passages.hearers:
Self-praise was common in Greek public life, but many writers also mocked it as vulgar. Paul plays on that. He calls his boasting foolish before he begins, and then he boasts of the wrong things.

Look closely at verse 20. It is a list of what the rival teachers did to the church. ‘Enslaves’: they made people serve them. ‘Exploits’: the word means to eat up, to devour; they lived off the church's money. ‘Takes advantage of you’: word for word, ‘takes’; they took from people what was not theirs. ‘Exalts himself’: they put themselves above others. ‘Strikes you in the face’: they humiliated people. In that world a slap in the face was a deep insult. Whether it was meant literally or as a picture, it was meant to shame.

And the church put up with it. Perhaps it looked like strength. Perhaps they thought a real man of God would act that way. Paul says, with heavy irony, that he was ‘too weak’ to treat them like that.
passages.ot:
The prophets condemned leaders who used God's people for gain. Ezekiel said of Israel's shepherds, “You eat the fat, wear the wool, and butcher the fattened sheep, but you do not feed the flock” (Ezekiel 34:3). “Instead, you have ruled them with violence and cruelty” (Ezekiel 34:4).

Jesus drew the line for his followers: “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their superiors exercise authority over them. It shall not be this way among you” (Matthew 20:25-26). Peter told church leaders to shepherd “not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3).
passages.hard:
What does verse 20 say about leaders who harm the people they lead?

It describes what is today called spiritual abuse, and these notes say so plainly. A leader who controls people's lives, takes their money, uses them, sets himself above them, or humiliates them is not acting for Christ, whatever gifts or titles he has. Paul says the church should never have put up with it. A leader who exploits, humiliates or controls is not to be obeyed. Paul's own authority, he says, was for ‘building you up, not tearing you down’ (13:10), and he called himself and his helpers ‘your servants for Jesus’ sake’ (4:5).

This is not about every leader who makes a mistake, or every hard word spoken in love. It is about a pattern of power used for oneself.

If you have been harmed by a controlling leader or church, what was done was wrong, and it was not your fault. Being taken in by someone who seemed godly is not a sign of weak faith; the Corinthians were taken in too. You are free to step away and to tell someone you trust. If you were abused in other ways, or a crime was done, it should be reported to the authorities. A pastor or counsellor outside that church may help you sort out what happened. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The Corinthians put up with leaders who used them, and doubted the one who served them. Ask what kind of leader you are drawn to, and why. If you lead anyone, ask whether the people under you are being built up or used. If you have been on the wrong end of such a leader, ask who you can safely talk to.

passages.t: ‘Five times I received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one’
passages.happening:
Paul now matches his rivals point by point. “Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they descendants of Abraham? So am I” (verse 22).

“Are they servants of Christ?” Here he says he is speaking as if out of his mind, “but I am so much more: in harder labor, in more imprisonments, in worse beatings, in frequent danger of death” (verse 23).

Then the list. “Five times I received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one. Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I was shipwrecked. I spent a night and a day in the open sea” (verses 24 and 25). He was in danger from rivers and bandits, from his own people and from Gentiles, in the city and in the country, at sea and among false brothers (verse 26). He knew hard work, sleepless nights, hunger, thirst, cold and exposure (verse 27).

And on top of all this, “I face daily the pressure of my concern for all the churches” (verse 28). “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is led into sin, and I do not burn with grief?” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
This list is a boast turned upside down. A Roman official might list his offices and honours. Paul lists his beatings.

Many of these sufferings are not in Acts. Acts tells of one beating with rods, at Philippi, where “the magistrates ordered that they be stripped and beaten with rods” (Acts 16:22). Paul says it happened three times. Beating with rods was a punishment given by Roman city officials, even though Paul was a Roman citizen (Acts 16:37). Acts tells of one stoning, at Lystra (Acts 14:19). The famous shipwreck of Acts 27 happened later than this letter, so it is not one of these three.

Count the word ‘danger’ in verse 26. In Greek it comes eight times. The rhythm hammers home a life lived without safety.

Then verse 28. After all the beatings, the heaviest weight is love: worry for the churches. Paul feels their weakness as his own.
passages.ot:
The forty lashes come from the Law of Moses. “If the guilty man deserves to be beaten, the judge shall have him lie down and be flogged in his presence with the number of lashes his crime warrants. He may receive no more than forty lashes, lest your brother be beaten any more than that and be degraded in your sight” (Deuteronomy 25:2-3). The limit protected the dignity of the one punished: he was still ‘your brother’. Later Jewish practice, written down in the Mishnah, gave thirty-nine, to be sure the limit was never passed. That is why Paul says ‘forty lashes minus one’.

The prophets knew what it was to suffer for God's word. Jeremiah was beaten and put in the stocks (Jeremiah 20:2). He cried, “I am a laughingstock all day long; everyone mocks me” (Jeremiah 20:7). Yet he could not stop: “His message becomes a fire burning in my heart, shut up in my bones” (Jeremiah 20:9).
passages.hard:
What does ‘five times I received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one’ mean, and is it a charge against the Jewish people?

It is not. These notes say so plainly. Paul was a Jew, as he has just said with pride (verse 22). The forty lashes minus one was a punishment given by a synagogue court to one of its own members. That Paul received it five times tells us something about him. He kept going to the synagogue to preach about Jesus, and he accepted its discipline rather than walk away from his own people. He wrote of them, “For I could wish that I myself were cursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my own flesh and blood” (Romans 9:3).

‘The Jews’ here means the synagogue leaders who judged him in certain towns, not the Jewish people as a whole. In the same verses Paul lists Roman beatings, Gentile dangers and false brothers in the church. He blames no people. The note on Acts 2:22-28 explains how verses like this were later misused against Jewish people, and why this site rejects that reading.
passages.asks: Paul's proof that he served Christ was not his success but what he had suffered and how much he cared. Ask what you would put on a list of your service, and what Paul's list says about it. Then think of someone whose weakness or failing you could carry with them, as Paul did.

passages.t: Down the wall in a basket
passages.happening:
Paul states his rule. “If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness” (verse 30). He calls God as his witness: “The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, who is forever worthy of praise, knows that I am not lying” (verse 31).

Then he tells a short story. “In Damascus, the governor under King Aretas secured the city of the Damascenes in order to arrest me. But I was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his grasp” (verses 32 and 33).
passages.hearers:
This happened soon after Paul came to faith. Acts tells the same escape (Acts 9:23-25). Aretas IV was king of the Nabataeans, an Arab kingdom east and south of Judea, from about 9 BC to AD 40. Historians debate how his officer had power in Damascus at that time. Acts names Paul's Jewish opponents in the city; Paul names the king's governor. Many readers think both were part of the same danger. The note on Acts 9:20-25 says more.

Why end the boasting here? The Romans gave a special crown, shaped like a city wall, to the first soldier to climb over an enemy's wall. Some readers think Paul's story plays on that: his great deed was going down a wall, in a basket, at night, running away. Others doubt the Corinthians would have thought of it. Either way, the story is meant to be humbling. It is the opposite of a hero's tale.
passages.ot:
Paul's escape has Old Testament likenesses. Rahab let Israel's spies down from her house on the city wall: “Then Rahab let them down by a rope through the window, since the house where she lived was built into the wall of the city” (Joshua 2:15). Michal helped David escape from Saul: “So Michal lowered David from the window, and he ran away and escaped” (1 Samuel 19:12).

In both stories, God's servants were saved not by strength but by a window and the help of others. So was Paul.
passages.asks: Paul chose to tell the story that made him look weakest. Ask what moment in your life you would least like others to know about, and whether God was at work in it all the same. Then ask who helped you over your ‘wall’, and whether you have thanked them.
